content: Hammer toe is a condition characterized by a deformity of the toe, where the end of the toe bends downward. Symptoms of Hammer Toe: The middle joint of the toe becomes bent. The end of the toe assumes a claw-like downward position. Initially, the toe may still be movable and can be straightened, but over time, it becomes fixed and immobile. Corns often develop on the top of the affected toe. Calluses may form on the sole of the foot. Walking or wearing shoes can become painful. Causes of Hammer Toe: Hammer toe most commonly affects the second toe but can involve other toes as well. The toe moves into a claw-like position due to various factors. The primary cause is wearing shoes that are too short, narrow, or tight, which forces the toe into a bent position. Over time, the muscles and tendons in the toe tighten and shorten, exacerbating the deformity. The condition can be congenital (present at birth) or develop gradually over time. In rare cases, all toes may be affected, which could indicate an underlying issue with the nerves or spinal cord. Risk Factors: Women who wear poorly fitting shoes or high heels are at higher risk. Children who continue to wear shoes they have outgrown are also more likely to develop hammer toe. Diagnosis: A physical examination of the foot is sufficient to confirm the presence of hammer toe. The healthcare provider may observe reduced and painful movement in the affected toes. When to Seek Medical Care: Schedule an appointment with a healthcare provider if: You need guidance on the best treatment options. Your pain worsens. You experience difficulty walking. Treatment Options: For mild cases in children: Manipulation and splinting of the affected toe can be effective. Footwear modifications: Wear properly fitting shoes with wide toe boxes to alleviate symptoms and prevent worsening of the condition. Avoid high heels as much as possible. Use soft insoles to reduce pressure on the toe. Protect the protruding joint with corn pads or felt pads. Orthotic devices: A podiatrist can create custom devices, such as hammer toe regulators or straighteners, or you can purchase them over the counter. Exercises: Gentle stretching exercises can help if the toe is not yet fixed in position. For example, picking up a towel with your toes can strengthen and stretch the small muscles in the foot. Surgical intervention: Severe cases may require surgery to straighten the joint. This often involves cutting or repositioning tendons and ligaments. In some cases, the bones on either side of the joint may need to be fused together. Most patients can return home the same day as the surgery, but the toe may remain stiff or shorter afterward. Where to Find Medical Care: Seek directions to hospitals or clinics that specialize in treating hammer toe. Prognosis: Early treatment can often prevent the need for surgery. Treatment typically reduces pain and improves walking ability. Possible Complications: Foot deformity. Postural changes due to difficulty walking. Prevention: Avoid wearing shoes that are too short or narrow. Regularly check children’s shoe sizes, especially during periods of rapid growth.
